steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on redundancy parameterization and inverse kinematics of 7-DOF revolute robot arms, centred on a generalized shoulder-elbow-wrist (SEW) angle that avoids the singularity problems of the conventional one.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. 7-DOF arms and redundancy / self-motion
2. The SEW angle as a redundancy parameterization
3. Algorithmic singularities: the weakness of the conventional SEW angle
4. Our approach: generalized and stereographic SEW angle
5. IK solutions for 7R robots
6. Contributions
7. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. 7-DOF arms and redundancy
- industrial arms: six revolute joints for 6 DOF of end effector pose; human arm 7 DOF (shoulder 3, elbow 1, wrist 3)
- 7R arms: RRC arm, Baxter, Sawyer, Yumi, SSRMS
- extra DOF -> continuum of configurations for one end effector pose
- self-motion: pose held constant, looks like elbow rotating about shoulder-wrist line (Figure 1)
- benefits over 6R: avoid singularities and obstacles, optimize motion time, avoid joint motion limits, avoid joint torque limits

2. SEW angle
- end effector pose must be augmented by a secondary task to fix pose up to finitely many solutions
- pure self-motion: parameterizations differ only in rate; differences clearer when end effector moves
- SEW angle (aka elbow angle): rotation of shoulder-elbow-wrist plane about shoulder-wrist line w.r.t. a reference plane
- reference plane conventionally = plane containing shoulder-wrist line + a reference vector
- easy to visualize, widely used in space teleoperation; intuitive for space robot operators
- some 7R arms: analytical IK (given pose + SEW angle, finite set of seven joint angles solved directly, not iteratively)
- augmented Jacobian: 7\times 7 matrix, joint velocity -> end effector spatial velocity + SEW angular velocity; easily characterized

3. Algorithmic singularities
- shoulder-wrist line collinear with reference vector -> reference plane undefined
- algorithmic singularity = due to choice of redundancy parameterization
- main weakness of SEW-like parameterizations; undesirable behavior near them like kinematic singularities
- dangerously large elbow movement, esp. bad for teleoperation
- poor convergence of iterative algorithms, numerical precision issues (many significant digits)
- designers must choose reference direction carefully; often wasted regions of reachable workspace

4. Our approach
- new generalized SEW angle, conventional one is a special case
- algorithmic singularity unavoidable for any redundancy parameterization
- stereographic projection choice: bidirectional singularity -> unidirectional
- singularity direction can point toward the arm base, outside workspace
- keeps SEW advantages: analytical IK for many 7R arms, intuitive teleoperation, analytical Jacobian
- existing algorithms using conventional SEW angle / Jacobian easily adapted

5. IK solutions
- IK with general SEW angle for most 7R robots in practice/literature, general 7R manipulators, arms that do not yet exist
- built on IK-Geo: open-source, easy-to-use, subproblem decomposition
- often closed-form; otherwise 1D or 2D search over compact set
- efficient, precise, stable vs Jacobian-based; robust to singularities; all solutions incl. singular, not just one near initial guess
- branches without exact solutions: continuous non-exact, sometimes least-squares solutions
- Cartesian motion through singularities, switching IK branches without joint control
- search-based -> polynomial solution: first polynomial in tangent half-angle of one joint for 7R robot parameterized by SEW angle

6. Contributions
- stereographic SEW angle: singularity only along half-line, not full line; much larger singularity-free region
- algorithmic singularities unavoidable; classify singularity types for 7R arms, when concurrent
- efficient IK for any 7R manipulator (conventional or stereographic SEW) via subproblem decomposition; categorize 7R robots by intersecting/parallel axes and shoulder, elbow, wrist choices; high-order polynomial in tangent half-angle of one joint

7. Organization
- Sec 2: related work, forward kinematics for 7R arms, coordinate-free notation, product of exponentials
- Sec 3: general SEW angle, forward and differential kinematics, singularity conditions, relation to conventional
- Sec 4: proof algorithmic singularities exist for any redundancy parameterization
- Sec 5: stereographic SEW angle, stereographic projection, singularity behavior, example comparing conventional vs stereographic
- Sec 6: IK solutions with examples; Sec 7: conclusion
- IK solutions, examples, evaluations in a public repository

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Most industrial robot arms have six revolute joints, which is enough to control the six degrees of freedom (DOF) of the end effector pose. A human arm though has seven DOF, three for the shoulder, one for the elbow, and three for the wrist. There are also 7-DOF revolute (7R) robot arms, for example the Robotics Research Corporation (RRC) arm, Baxter, Sawyer, Yumi, and the Space Station Robot Manipulator System (SSRMS). Because of the extra redundant degree of freedom there is a continuum of arm configurations for a given hand or end effector pose. If the end effector pose is held constant and the arm moves through this continuum, which is called self-motion, it usually looks like the elbow is rotating around the line from the shoulder to the wrist (Figure 1). 7R arms have benefits over 6R arms since the redundancy can be used to avoid singularities and obstacles, to optimize motion time, to avoid joint motion limits, and to avoid joint torque limits.

To fully specify the pose of a 7R robot up to a finite number of solutions, a secondary task has to be added to the end effector pose. In pure self-motion the only difference between parameterizations would be how fast things move, and the differences between parameterizations are clearer when the end effector is moving. For human arms and many 7R robot arms, the redundancy can be conveniently parameterized by the shoulder-elbow-wrist (SEW) angle, which is sometimes called the elbow angle. It describes the rotation of the plane that contains the shoulder, elbow, and wrist about the shoulder-wrist line, relative to a reference plane. The reference plane is usually chosen as the plane containing the shoulder-wrist line and a reference vector. This parameterization is easy to visualize and it is widely used, for example in space teleoperation, partly because it is intuitive for space robot operators. Also, for certain 7R arms the inverse kinematics has an analytical solution, which means that for a given end effector pose and SEW angle the finite set of the seven joint angles can be solved directly and not iteratively. The augmented Jacobian, which is the 7\times 7 matrix mapping the joint velocity vector to the end effector spatial velocity and the SEW angular velocity, is also easy to characterize.

There is an issue with the conventional SEW angle when the shoulder-wrist line is collinear with the reference vector, because then the reference plane is undefined. This is called an algorithmic singularity, meaning a singularity that comes from the choice of redundancy parameterization. Algorithmic singularities are the main weakness of parameterizations like the SEW angle because robots behave badly near them, the same as near kinematic singularities. For example being near an algorithmic singularity may cause dangerously large elbow movement, which is especially a problem for teleoperation. It also causes poor convergence for iterative algorithms and numerical precision problems, since many significant digits are needed to specify the robot pose accurately. Designers have to choose the reference direction carefully to avoid singularities, but often it is inevitable that regions of the reachable workspace are wasted.

[Our approach]
- generalized SEW angle, conventional is special case
- algorithmic singularity unavoidable for any parameterization; stereographic choice -> unidirectional instead of bidirectional
- singularity toward arm base, not in workspace
- keeps analytical IK, intuitive teleoperation, analytical Jacobian; existing algorithms easily adapted

[IK solutions]
- general SEW angle IK for most 7R robots, general 7R, arms not yet existing; built on IK-Geo (open-source, subproblem decomposition)
- closed-form often, else 1D/2D search over compact set; efficient, precise, stable; all solutions incl. singular
- non-exact / least-squares solutions for branches without exact solutions -> Cartesian motion through singularities
- first polynomial in tangent half-angle of one joint for 7R robot with SEW angle

[Contributions]
- stereographic SEW angle: half-line singularity instead of full line
- algorithmic singularities unavoidable; classify singularity types, concurrency
- IK for any 7R manipulator via subproblem decomposition; categorize robots; high-order polynomial

[Organization]
- Sec 2 related work + forward kinematics; Sec 3 general SEW angle; Sec 4 existence proof; Sec 5 stereographic SEW angle + example; Sec 6 IK; Sec 7 conclusion
- public repository with IK solutions, examples, evaluations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Most industrial robot arms have six revolute joints, which is enough to control the six degrees of freedom (DOF) of the end effector pose. A human arm though has seven DOF, three for the shoulder, one for the elbow, and three for the wrist. There are also 7-DOF revolute (7R) robot arms, for example the Robotics Research Corporation (RRC) arm, Baxter, Sawyer, Yumi, and the Space Station Robot Manipulator System (SSRMS). Because of the extra redundant degree of freedom there is a continuum of arm configurations for a given hand or end effector pose. If the end effector pose is held constant and the arm moves through this continuum, which is called self-motion, it usually looks like the elbow is rotating around the line from the shoulder to the wrist (Figure 1). 7R arms have benefits over 6R arms since the redundancy can be used to avoid singularities and obstacles, to optimize motion time, to avoid joint motion limits, and to avoid joint torque limits.

To fully specify the pose of a 7R robot up to a finite number of solutions, a secondary task has to be added to the end effector pose. In pure self-motion the only difference between parameterizations would be how fast things move, and the differences between parameterizations are clearer when the end effector is moving. For human arms and many 7R robot arms, the redundancy can be conveniently parameterized by the shoulder-elbow-wrist (SEW) angle, which is sometimes called the elbow angle. It describes the rotation of the plane that contains the shoulder, elbow, and wrist about the shoulder-wrist line, relative to a reference plane. The reference plane is usually chosen as the plane containing the shoulder-wrist line and a reference vector. This parameterization is easy to visualize and it is widely used, for example in space teleoperation, partly because it is intuitive for space robot operators. Also, for certain 7R arms the inverse kinematics has an analytical solution, which means that for a given end effector pose and SEW angle the finite set of the seven joint angles can be solved directly and not iteratively. The augmented Jacobian, which is the 7\times 7 matrix mapping the joint velocity vector to the end effector spatial velocity and the SEW angular velocity, is also easy to characterize.

There is an issue with the conventional SEW angle when the shoulder-wrist line is collinear with the reference vector, because then the reference plane is undefined. This is called an algorithmic singularity, meaning a singularity that comes from the choice of redundancy parameterization. Algorithmic singularities are the main weakness of parameterizations like the SEW angle because robots behave badly near them, the same as near kinematic singularities. For example being near an algorithmic singularity may cause dangerously large elbow movement, which is especially a problem for teleoperation. It also causes poor convergence for iterative algorithms and numerical precision problems, since many significant digits are needed to specify the robot pose accurately. Designers have to choose the reference direction carefully to avoid singularities, but often it is inevitable that regions of the reachable workspace are wasted.

In this paper we introduce a new generalized concept of SEW angle, and the conventional SEW angle is a special case of it. We show that an algorithmic singularity can't be avoided for any redundancy parameterization, but a special choice of the generalized SEW angle that is based on the stereographic projection changes the bidirectional singularity into a unidirectional singularity. The singularity direction can be placed towards the base of the arm so it is not encountered in the robot workspace. The generalized SEW angle still keeps the advantages of the SEW angle redundancy parameterization, such as analytical inverse kinematics for many 7R arms, intuitive teleoperation, and an analytical Jacobian. Most existing algorithms that use the conventional SEW angle or its Jacobian can easily be adapted to use the general SEW angle, and this includes the stereographic SEW angle.

We also give inverse kinematics (IK) solutions using the general SEW angle for most 7R robots used in practice or mentioned in the literature, including general 7R manipulators and also arms which do not exist yet. The solutions are built on IK-Geo, which is an open-source and easy-to-use IK solver based on a unifying subproblem decomposition approach. The solutions are often closed-form, but for some robots IK is solved with a 1D or 2D search over a compact set. These analytical and semi-analytical methods are efficient, precise, and stable, especially compared to Jacobian-based algorithms. They are also robust to singularities and they find all IK solutions, including singular solution, and not just one close to an initial guess. For branches that don't have exact solutions they return continuous non-exact and sometimes least-squares solutions. This means Cartesian motion can go directly through singularities and switch between IK branches without using joint control. We also show how to convert a search-based solution to a polynomial solution. To the best of our knowledge we are the first to give a polynomial in the tangent half-angle of one joint which corresponds to IK solutions of a 7R robot parameterized by SEW angle.

The new contributions in this paper are:

- We introduce the stereographic SEW angle, a new redundancy parameterization which has a singularity only along a half-line and not a full line like the conventional SEW angle. This makes the singularity-free region of the workspace a lot bigger.

- We show that algorithmic singularities can't be avoided for any redundancy parameterization. We classify the different types of singularities for 7R arms and discuss when singularities are concurrent.

- We solve IK efficiently for any 7R manipulator parameterized by the conventional or stereographic SEW angle using the subproblem decomposition approach. We categorize 7R robots by intersecting or parallel axes and by the choice of shoulder, elbow, and wrist locations. We also show solving IK for a 7R manipulator parameterized by conventional or stereographic SEW angle by finding a high-order polynomial in the tangent half-angle of one joint.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 discusses previous related work and describes forward kinematics for 7R arms with coordinate-free notation and the product of exponentials approach. Section 3 introduces the general SEW angle including forward and differential kinematics, discusses singularity conditions, and relates it to the conventional SEW angle. Section 4 proves that algorithmic singularities exist for any redundancy parameterization. Section 5 defines the stereographic SEW angle, discusses how it relates to stereographic projection and how its singularities behave, and gives an example comparing the conventional and stereographic SEW angle formulations. Section 6 gives IK solutions with examples, and Section 7 concludes.

The inverse kinematics solutions, examples, and evaluations are available in a publicly accessible repository.

In the same way, there are 7-DOF revolute (7R) robot arms such as the Robotics Research Corporation (RRC) arm [1], Baxter [2], Sawyer [3], Yumi [4], and the Space Station Robot Manipulator System (SSRMS) [5]. Because of the extra redundant degree of freedom, there is a continuum of arm configurations for a given hand or robot end effector pose. Holding the end effector pose constant while moving through this continuum of arm configurations, called self-motion, usually looks like the elbow rotating around the line passing from the shoulder to the wrist (Figure 1). Benefits of 7R arms over 6R arms include using redundancy to avoid singularities and obstacles [6], optimize motion time [7], avoid joint motion limits [8], and avoid joint torque limits [9].

To fully specify the pose of a 7R robot up to a finite number of solutions, the end effector pose must be augmented by a secondary task. During pure self-motion the only difference between parameterizations would be the rate of movement; the differences between parameterizations become clearer during motion of the end effector. Redundancy in human and many 7R robot arms can be conveniently parameterized by the shoulder-elbow-wrist (SEW) angle, sometimes called the elbow angle, which characterizes the rotation of the plane containing the shoulder, elbow, and wrist about the shoulder-wrist line with respect to a reference plane. This reference plane is conventionally chosen as the plane containing the shoulder-wrist line and a reference vector. This redundancy parameterization is easy to visualize and is widely used in applications such as space teleoperation [10,11,12], partly because it is intuitive for space robot operators [13]. In addition, for certain 7R arms the inverse kinematics has an analytical solution, i.e., for a given robot end effector pose and SEW angle, the finite set of the seven robot joint angles can be solved directly rather than iteratively. The augmented Jacobian, the 7\times 7 matrix that maps the joint velocity vector to the end effector spatial velocity and the SEW angular velocity, is easily characterized.

An issue with the conventional SEW angle appears when the shoulder-wrist line is collinear with the reference vector, because the reference plane then becomes undefined. This is referred to as an algorithmic singularity, a singularity due to the choice of redundancy parameterization. Algorithmic singularities are the main weakness of parameterizations like the SEW angle [14] because robots show undesirable behavior near them just as near kinematic singularities. For example, being near an algorithmic singularity may result in dangerously large elbow movement, which is especially problematic for teleoperation [10]. It also leads to poor convergence for iterative algorithms and to numerical precision problems, since many significant digits are required to specify the robot pose accurately. Designers must carefully choose the reference direction to avoid singularities, but wasting regions of the reachable workspace is often inevitable [15,16,17,18].

In this paper, we introduce a new generalized concept of SEW angle which includes the conventional SEW angle as a special case. We show that an algorithmic singularity is unavoidable for any redundancy parameterization, but that a special choice of the generalized SEW angle based on the stereographic projection changes the bidirectional singularity into a unidirectional singularity. The singularity direction can be located towards the base of the arm so that it is not encountered in the robot workspace. The generalized SEW angle retains the advantages of the SEW angle redundancy parameterization, including analytical inverse kinematics for many 7R arms, intuitive teleoperation, and an analytical Jacobian. Most existing algorithms which use the conventional SEW angle or its Jacobian can be easily adapted to use the general SEW angle, including the stereographic SEW angle.

We also provide inverse kinematics (IK) solutions using the general SEW angle for most 7R robots used in practice or mentioned in the literature, including general 7R manipulators as well as arms which do not yet exist. These solutions build upon IK-Geo, an open-source and easy-to-use IK solver based on a unifying subproblem decomposition approach [19]. The solutions are often closed-form, but for some robots IK is solved using a 1D or 2D search over a compact set. These analytical and semi-analytical methods are efficient, precise, and stable, especially compared to Jacobian-based algorithms. They are also robust to singularities and find all IK solutions, including singular solution, rather than only one close to an initial guess. For branches without exact solutions, they return continuous non-exact and sometimes least-squares solutions, which allows Cartesian motion directly through singularities to switch between different IK branches without resorting to joint control. We also demonstrate converting a search-based solution to a polynomial solution: to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide a polynomial in the tangent half-angle of one joint which corresponds to IK solutions of a 7R robot parameterized by SEW angle.

We offer the following new contributions in this paper:

- We introduce the stereographic SEW angle, a new redundancy parameterization that encounters a singularity only along a half-line rather than a full line as in the conventional SEW angle. This significantly enlarges the singularity-free region of the workspace.

- We show that algorithmic singularities are unavoidable for any redundancy parameterization. We classify the different types of singularities for 7R arms and discuss when singularities are concurrent.

- We efficiently solve IK for any 7R manipulator parameterized by the conventional or stereographic SEW angle using the subproblem decomposition approach. We categorize 7R robots based on intersecting or parallel axes and on choices of shoulder, elbow, and wrist locations. We also demonstrate solving IK for a 7R manipulator parameterized by conventional or stereographic SEW angle by finding a high-order polynomial in the tangent half-angle of one joint.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we discuss previous related work and describe forward kinematics for 7R arms using coordinate-free notation and the product of exponentials approach. In Section 3 we introduce the general SEW angle, including forward and differential kinematics, discuss singularity conditions, and relate it to the conventional SEW angle. In Section 4 we prove the existence of algorithmic singularities for any redundancy parameterization. In Section 5 we define the stereographic SEW angle, discuss its relationship to stereographic projection and its singularity behavior, and give an example comparing the conventional and stereographic SEW angle formulations. We provide IK solutions with examples in Section 6 and conclude in Section 7.

Inverse kinematics solutions, examples, and evaluations are available in a publicly accessible repository.
